opus-5.5.text:
I think that judgment was partly right and partly a reflection of where I was personally at that time.

When I was finishing my PhD at MIT, I felt that a lot of graphics research had become very incremental. In physical simulation, for example, many papers were about making a specific phenomenon a bit more accurate, or a method a few times faster on a specific benchmark. Those are real contributions, but the gap between what we published and what people actually used in industry felt quite large. A beautiful SIGGRAPH paper might get cited, but very few people would actually put it into a production pipeline, because the engineering cost was too high. That was one of the reasons I worked on Taichi in the first place. I felt the bottleneck wasn't only algorithms, it was also the tools, the productivity of turning ideas into working, high-performance code.

Looking back, I'd say I was right that traditional graphics, in the sense of hand-designed algorithms for rendering and simulation, was approaching diminishing returns as an academic field. But I underestimated how quickly the field would be reshaped from the outside. Neural rendering, NeRF, Gaussian splatting, generative models for images, video, and 3D: these brought a huge amount of new energy into graphics. So it wasn't that graphics was dead. It was that the next big wave would come from combining graphics with learning and with large-scale compute, rather than from pushing the classic methods a little further.

So if I evaluate my younger self honestly, the diagnosis of a bottleneck was reasonable, but I was perhaps a bit too pessimistic about the field as a whole. A bottleneck in one paradigm often means a new paradigm is about to show up. The more useful lesson for me was this: when you feel a field is saturating, don't just leave. Ask what's missing, whether that's tools, infrastructure, or a new way of thinking, and see whether you can be the one to build it.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I'd say that judgment was half right and half wrong, and the half I got wrong is the more interesting part.

When I was finishing my PhD, the feeling was very concrete. I had spent years on physical simulation, on things like MPM solvers and differentiable simulation, and the papers were getting more and more incremental. You'd spend six months to get a 20 percent speedup on a problem that maybe ten people in the world cared about. The field was mature. The low-hanging fruit was gone. SIGGRAPH papers were beautiful, but the gap between a beautiful paper and something people actually used in production was enormous, and it wasn't shrinking. So I concluded that graphics research as an academic discipline had hit a plateau, and that if I wanted real impact, I should go build tools rather than write more papers. That's part of why Taichi became a company instead of just a thesis project.

That part I still stand by. The tooling problem was real. Writing high-performance simulation code was painful, and lowering that barrier mattered.

What I got wrong was the framing. I thought "graphics" was the thing, and that the thing was stagnating. But the underlying skills, differentiable programming, writing compilers for parallel hardware, thinking about how to express physics efficiently on GPUs, those turned out to be exactly what the next wave needed. Neural rendering, 3D generation, simulation for robotics, all of that exploded within a couple of years. The bottleneck wasn't the field. It was that the field was about to be absorbed into something bigger, and I was looking at it from the inside and mistaking a transition for a dead end.

So if a student asked me today, I'd say be careful about declaring a field finished. Usually what you're feeling is that the current set of questions is exhausted, not that the underlying capabilities are. The honest assessment of my younger self is that I had good instincts about what to go build, but I was a bit too confident about why.

astra-6.text:
I’d qualify that judgment today. When I graduated, I felt that some of the computer graphics problems I was working on had reached a point where further improvements required a lot of effort but made a relatively small difference. At the time, I interpreted that as a bottleneck for the field. Looking back, that was probably too broad a conclusion.

There’s a difference between a research direction becoming mature and an entire field running out of opportunities. You can keep improving an existing method, but you can also change the assumptions, the tools, or the problem you’re trying to solve. Those changes can open up a much larger space.

So I think my judgment was useful as a signal about what I wanted to work on next, but less reliable as a prediction about computer graphics as a whole. I’d now ask, “Where can we make a meaningful difference?” rather than, “Has this field reached its limit?”

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think that judgment was too broad. It was less that computer graphics had reached a bottleneck and more that I was feeling diminishing returns in the particular problems I was working on. Those are different things.

When you spend years inside a field, you become very aware of what is difficult to improve, and it’s easy to mistake the limits of your own perspective for the limits of the field. So I would separate two questions: Was graphics running out of opportunities? And was it the right time for me to explore something else? I could be wrong about the first and still make a reasonable decision about the second.

Today, I would be much more cautious about declaring that an entire research field has hit a ceiling.
